items.stem:
Read the following text.

Zeus looked down at humans and saw only cruelty, so he sent rain until the whole world drowned.
Only Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survived, floating in a wooden chest until it came to rest on Mount Parnassus.
Alone and afraid, they prayed. A voice told them: 'Throw the bones of your mother over your shoulders.'
Pyrrha was horrified – until Deucalion understood. Their mother was the Earth; her bones were stones. Every stone they threw became a person, and the world was full again.

This text is best classified as a:
options: myth
news report
advertisement
biography extract
items.answer: myth
items.markingKey: A. It is a myth: it uses conventions such as gods or supernatural beings, a hero, a quest or test, and an explanation of how something in nature or society began.

items.stem: Explain why myths can tell us about the values of the culture that created them.
items.answer: The heroes, rewards and punishments in a myth show what a culture admired or feared – for example, the Manu story rewards kindness, and the Greek flood punishes cruelty.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The heroes, rewards and punishments in a myth show what a culture admired or feared – for example, the Manu story rewards kindness, and the Greek flood punishes cruelty. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a fable and a myth.
items.answer: A myth explains origins or beliefs through gods and heroes; a fable is a short story, often with animals, that teaches a clear moral lesson.
items.markingKey: A myth explains origins or beliefs through gods and heroes; a fable is a short story, often with animals, that teaches a clear moral lesson. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following retelling of the Chinese creation myth of Pangu.

In the beginning there was only a great egg, and inside it slept Pangu.
For eighteen thousand years he grew, until one day he stretched and the egg cracked open. The light, clear parts floated up and became the sky; the heavy, dark parts sank and became the earth.
Afraid they would join again, Pangu stood between them, pushing the sky higher each day.
When at last he died, his breath became the wind, his voice the thunder, his eyes the sun and moon, and his blood the rivers.

Explain which features of this text are typical of traditional stories.
items.answer: It has a supernatural being (the giant Pangu), a time "in the beginning", huge time-scales (eighteen thousand years) and it explains how the natural world began – sky, earth, wind, thunder, sun, moon and rivers.
items.markingKey: It has a supernatural being (the giant Pangu), a time "in the beginning", huge time-scales (eighteen thousand years) and it explains how the natural world began – sky, earth, wind, thunder, sun, moon and rivers. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Name the natural feature that each of these mythical explanations is about: (a) Rangi's tears; (b) Papa's sighs; (c) Pangu's blood.
items.answer: (a) rain; (b) morning mist; (c) rivers.
items.markingKey: (a) rain; (b) morning mist; (c) rivers.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Myths are still relevant to teenagers today."
items.answer: Myths remain relevant because their patterns and themes still shape stories and help us explore what it means to be human, even if we no longer read them as explanations of nature.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: modern films and books (superhero stories, fantasy) use mythical heroes and quests; myths explore universal themes like courage, family and loss. Arguments against: science now explains nature; some myths reflect old-fashioned values. Supported judgement: Myths remain relevant because their patterns and themes still shape stories and help us explore what it means to be human, even if we no longer read them as explanations of nature.

items.stem:
Read the following retelling of the Polynesian story of Māui and the sun.

In the old days the sun raced across the sky so fast that there was never enough daylight to cook food or finish work.
Māui's brothers laughed when he said he would slow it down. But Māui had a jawbone given to him by his grandmother, full of magic.
With his brothers he wove ropes from flax, travelled east to the sun's pit and waited all night.
When the sun rose, they snared it. Māui beat it with the jawbone until, weak and limping, it promised to travel slowly. And so we have long days.

Which technique is used in "weak and limping, it promised to travel slowly"?
options: onomatopoeia
statistic
simile
personification
items.answer: personification
items.markingKey: D. "weak and limping, it promised to travel slowly" is an example of personification: the sun is treated as a creature that can be defeated, making the cosmic task feel like a physical fight.

items.stem:
Read the following retelling of the Greek flood myth of Deucalion and Pyrrha.

Zeus looked down at humans and saw only cruelty, so he sent rain until the whole world drowned.
Only Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survived, floating in a wooden chest until it came to rest on Mount Parnassus.
Alone and afraid, they prayed. A voice told them: 'Throw the bones of your mother over your shoulders.'
Pyrrha was horrified – until Deucalion understood. Their mother was the Earth; her bones were stones. Every stone they threw became a person, and the world was full again.

What does this story suggest about the values of the culture that created it?
items.answer: It shows Greek ideas that the gods punish wickedness and reward piety, and that humans are connected to the Earth ("Mother").
items.markingKey: It shows Greek ideas that the gods punish wickedness and reward piety, and that humans are connected to the Earth ("Mother"). Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "hero's journey"?
options: A common story pattern, described by Joseph Campbell, in which a hero leaves the ordinary world, faces tests and returns transformed with a reward
A traditional story, often sacred to a culture, involving gods or supernatural beings, that explains the origins of the world, nature or customs
A traditional story about a hero or event linked to a real place or historical time, with exaggerated or supernatural elements
The passing down of stories by word of mouth from one generation to the next, before or alongside writing
items.answer: A common story pattern, described by Joseph Campbell, in which a hero leaves the ordinary world, faces tests and returns transformed with a reward
items.markingKey: A. "hero's journey" is a common story pattern, described by Joseph Campbell, in which a hero leaves the ordinary world, faces tests and returns transformed with a reward.

items.stem:
Read the following retelling of the Greek flood myth of Deucalion and Pyrrha.

Zeus looked down at humans and saw only cruelty, so he sent rain until the whole world drowned.
Only Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survived, floating in a wooden chest until it came to rest on Mount Parnassus.
Alone and afraid, they prayed. A voice told them: 'Throw the bones of your mother over your shoulders.'
Pyrrha was horrified – until Deucalion understood. Their mother was the Earth; her bones were stones. Every stone they threw became a person, and the world was full again.

Describe the tone of the text and explain how the writer creates it.
items.answer: The tone is dramatic and solemn: divine anger and fear create drama; the ending brings hope.
items.markingKey: The tone is dramatic and solemn: divine anger and fear create drama; the ending brings hope. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Explain why the hero usually returns home at the end of the journey.
items.answer: The return shows that the hero has changed and brings back a reward (knowledge, a gift, safety) that benefits the community, giving the journey its purpose.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The return shows that the hero has changed and brings back a reward (knowledge, a gift, safety) that benefits the community, giving the journey its purpose. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Map the legend of Sundiata onto three stages of the hero's journey.
items.answer: Ordinary world: he cannot walk and is mocked. Call/threshold: his mother is insulted and he stands with the iron rod. Later ordeal and return: exile, defeat of Soumaoro and founding of the Mali Empire.
items.markingKey: Ordinary world: he cannot walk and is mocked. Call/threshold: his mother is insulted and he stands with the iron rod. Later ordeal and return: exile, defeat of Soumaoro and founding of the Mali Empire.

items.stem: Amara writes: "The mentor is always an old man with a beard." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A mentor can be anyone – a grandmother (Māui), a friend, an animal or even a voice – who guides the hero.
items.markingKey: A mentor can be anyone – a grandmother (Māui), a friend, an animal or even a voice – who guides the hero. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Plan a hero's journey story set in your own town: list six stages with one sentence for each.
items.answer: Indicative content: six clearly named stages in a logical order (ordinary world, call, refusal, mentor, ordeal, return); a consistent hero and setting; a reward that changes the hero or community.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: six clearly named stages in a logical order (ordinary world, call, refusal, mentor, ordeal, return); a consistent hero and setting; a reward that changes the hero or community.

items.stem:
Read the following modern myth written by a Grade 8 student, "Why the City Never Sleeps".

When the city was young, it slept every night like everyone else.
But the Night Spirit was lonely. She drifted through empty streets, whispering to the closed shops.
One night a baker's daughter, Ines, heard her crying. 'I'll keep you company,' Ines said, and she lit one lamp in her window.
The Spirit was so grateful that she breathed light into every window, every street and every sign.
And that is why the city never sleeps: it is keeping a lonely spirit company.

How would you describe the writer's tone? Refer to two language choices that create it.
items.answer: The tone is gentle and magical: simple storytelling and kindness create a gentle mood.
items.markingKey: The tone is gentle and magical: simple storytelling and kindness create a gentle mood. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following retelling of the West African legend of Sundiata, the Lion King of Mali.

Sundiata was born in Niani, in the land of Mali, but he could not walk. For years other children mocked him and his mother wept.
One day the queen insulted his mother because Sundiata could not bring her baobab leaves. That evening, Sundiata asked for an iron rod. Leaning on it, he pulled himself up – and the rod bent like a bow.
He walked to the baobab tree, uprooted it and laid it at his mother's door.
Years later, Sundiata would return from exile to defeat the sorcerer-king Soumaoro and found the Mali Empire.

How does the legend show Sundiata changing from a weak child into a hero?
Write a PEE paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers the question.
items.answer: At first Sundiata is presented as powerless – he "could not walk" and is "mocked". The insult to his mother becomes his call to action. The simile "the rod bent like a bow" shows superhuman strength and hints he will be a warrior, and uprooting the baobab is an extraordinary deed done out of love. The foreshadowing of his return from exile shows this is the beginning of a hero's journey.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: At first Sundiata is presented as powerless – he "could not walk" and is "mocked". The insult to his mother becomes his call to action. The simile "the rod bent like a bow" shows superhuman strength and hints he will be a warrior, and uprooting the baobab is an extraordinary deed done out of love. The foreshadowing of his return from exile shows this is the beginning of a hero's journey. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "creation myth"?
options: A myth that explains how the world, the universe or people came into being
A myth in which a great flood destroys the world and a chosen survivor allows life to begin again
The passing down of stories by word of mouth from one generation to the next, before or alongside writing
The "voice" telling a story; myths often use a third-person storyteller's voice
items.answer: A myth that explains how the world, the universe or people came into being
items.markingKey: A. "creation myth" is a myth that explains how the world, the universe or people came into being.

items.stem: Briefly explain why flood myths appear in many different cultures.
items.answer: Many early civilisations lived near rivers and coasts and experienced devastating floods; the flood story also expresses the idea of cleansing and a new beginning.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many early civilisations lived near rivers and coasts and experienced devastating floods; the flood story also expresses the idea of cleansing and a new beginning. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Complete the comparison: "In the Pangu myth, the world is made from ______, whereas in the Māori story, rain and mist are explained as ______."
items.answer: Pangu's body (breath, voice, eyes, blood); the tears and sighs of the separated Sky Father and Earth Mother.
items.markingKey: Pangu's body (breath, voice, eyes, blood); the tears and sighs of the separated Sky Father and Earth Mother.

items.stem:
Read the following retelling of the Maori creation story of Rangi and Papa.

Long ago, Ranginui the Sky Father and Papatūānuku the Earth Mother held each other so tightly that their children lived in darkness between them.
The children argued. One wanted to kill their parents. Tāne, god of the forests, had a better idea.
He lay on his back, pressed his feet against his father and pushed – slowly, for a very long time – until the sky rose and light flooded in.
Rangi's tears for his lost wife still fall as rain, and Papa's sighs rise as morning mist.

What question about the world does this myth answer?
items.answer: Why there is light between earth and sky, and why it rains (Rangi's tears) and why mist rises (Papa's sighs).
items.markingKey: Why there is light between earth and sky, and why it rains (Rangi's tears) and why mist rises (Papa's sighs). Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Text A: retelling of the Chinese creation myth of Pangu.

In the beginning there was only a great egg, and inside it slept Pangu.
For eighteen thousand years he grew, until one day he stretched and the egg cracked open. The light, clear parts floated up and became the sky; the heavy, dark parts sank and became the earth.
Afraid they would join again, Pangu stood between them, pushing the sky higher each day.
When at last he died, his breath became the wind, his voice the thunder, his eyes the sun and moon, and his blood the rivers.

Text B: retelling of the Maori creation story of Rangi and Papa.

Long ago, Ranginui the Sky Father and Papatūānuku the Earth Mother held each other so tightly that their children lived in darkness between them.
The children argued. One wanted to kill their parents. Tāne, god of the forests, had a better idea.
He lay on his back, pressed his feet against his father and pushed – slowly, for a very long time – until the sky rose and light flooded in.
Rangi's tears for his lost wife still fall as rain, and Papa's sighs rise as morning mist.

Compare how the two creation myths explain the separation of the sky and the earth. In your answer, refer closely to both texts and use comparative connectives.
items.answer: In both myths the sky and earth were once joined and a powerful being pushes them apart. Text A (Chinese) presents one giant, Pangu, whose own body becomes nature after his death (sacrifice); Text B (Maori) presents a family – the Sky Father and Earth Mother – separated by their son Tāne. Text A emphasises effort and transformation (a list of body parts becoming nature); Text B emphasises love and loss through personification (rain as tears, mist as sighs). Both explain natural features and show that people and nature are connected.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: In both myths the sky and earth were once joined and a powerful being pushes them apart. Text A (Chinese) presents one giant, Pangu, whose own body becomes nature after his death (sacrifice); Text B (Maori) presents a family – the Sky Father and Earth Mother – separated by their son Tāne. Text A emphasises effort and transformation (a list of body parts becoming nature); Text B emphasises love and loss through personification (rain as tears, mist as sighs). Both explain natural features and show that people and nature are connected. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling. Comparison must be sustained across both texts (criterion B).

items.stem: "Cultures with similar myths must have copied each other." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Similar myths can develop independently because people everywhere face similar experiences (floods, darkness, the sky) and ask similar questions.
items.markingKey: Similar myths can develop independently because people everywhere face similar experiences (floods, darkness, the sky) and ask similar questions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which ending best shows the conventions of an origin myth?
items.answer: "And that is why phones grow warm when you hold them for too long."
items.markingKey: "And that is why phones grow warm when you hold them for too long.". Origin myths end by explaining something.

items.stem: Distinguish between a modern myth and a traditional myth.
items.answer: A traditional myth was passed down orally within a culture and expresses its sacred beliefs; a modern myth is written by an individual today, borrowing myth conventions to explain or comment on something in the modern world.
items.markingKey: A traditional myth was passed down orally within a culture and expresses its sacred beliefs; a modern myth is written by an individual today, borrowing myth conventions to explain or comment on something in the modern world. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "A modern myth does not need any supernatural elements." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Supernatural beings or forces are a key convention of myth; without them it is simply a realistic story.
items.markingKey: Supernatural beings or forces are a key convention of myth; without them it is simply a realistic story. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following modern myth written by a Grade 8 student, "Why the City Never Sleeps".

When the city was young, it slept every night like everyone else.
But the Night Spirit was lonely. She drifted through empty streets, whispering to the closed shops.
One night a baker's daughter, Ines, heard her crying. 'I'll keep you company,' Ines said, and she lit one lamp in her window.
The Spirit was so grateful that she breathed light into every window, every street and every sign.
And that is why the city never sleeps: it is keeping a lonely spirit company.

Identify two myth conventions that this writer uses, and suggest one more convention you would add if you rewrote it.
items.answer: It copies the conventions of a traditional myth – "When the city was young", a spirit, a kind human, a gift and an ending that explains something ("And that is why...") – but applies them to a modern city.
items.markingKey: It copies the conventions of a traditional myth – "When the city was young", a spirit, a kind human, a gift and an ending that explains something ("And that is why...") – but applies them to a modern city. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: two hands, one old and one young, holding the same chess piece above a board in a park in Moscow.]

Write a descriptive paragraph (about 150 words) that recreates this scene using at least three senses.
items.answer: Indicative content: establishes a tense but affectionate mood; possible idea – a final game between a grandfather and grandson, a rivalry between strangers, or passing on a skill; techniques such as symbolism of the game, dialogue, a pause before the climax; a hook that raises a question.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: establishes a tense but affectionate mood; possible idea – a final game between a grandfather and grandson, a rivalry between strangers, or passing on a skill; techniques such as symbolism of the game, dialogue, a pause before the climax; a hook that raises a question. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

Read the following retelling of the Polynesian story of Māui and the sun.

In the old days the sun raced across the sky so fast that there was never enough daylight to cook food or finish work.
Māui's brothers laughed when he said he would slow it down. But Māui had a jawbone given to him by his grandmother, full of magic.

Retell the Māui story as a short comic-strip script of four panels (describe each image and write the speech bubbles and captions).

items.stem: Explain why a writer might use the hero's journey when writing a modern myth.
items.answer: It gives a clear, satisfying structure (call, test, return) that readers recognise, so the writer can focus on making the setting and hero original.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It gives a clear, satisfying structure (call, test, return) that readers recognise, so the writer can focus on making the setting and hero original. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Write a modern myth (about 400 words) that explains a feature of your town or city, using the stages of the hero's journey.
items.answer: Indicative content: formulaic opening; supernatural being; a hero with a call and a test; the hero's journey structure; vivid description; an "And that is why..." ending. Criteria B, C, D.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: formulaic opening; supernatural being; a hero with a call and a test; the hero's journey structure; vivid description; an "And that is why..." ending. Criteria B, C, D.

items.stem: In the Polynesian story, what does Māui do to the sun?
options: He marries it
He snares it and forces it to travel more slowly
He steals it and hides it in a cave
He turns it into the moon
items.answer: He snares it and forces it to travel more slowly
items.markingKey: B. The story explains the length of the day.

items.answer: A common story pattern, described by Joseph Campbell, in which a hero leaves the ordinary world, faces tests and returns transformed with a reward

items.stem: Explain the difference between the Greek flood myth and the Hindu flood myth of Manu.
items.answer: In the Greek myth, Zeus sends the flood to punish human cruelty and survivors must solve a riddle; in the Manu story, the flood is a coming disaster and Manu is saved because he was kind to a small fish.
items.markingKey: In the Greek myth, Zeus sends the flood to punish human cruelty and survivors must solve a riddle; in the Manu story, the flood is a coming disaster and Manu is saved because he was kind to a small fish. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "Myths are just lies, so they have no value." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Myths are not meant as factual reports; they express a culture's beliefs, values and ways of understanding the world, and they still shape literature, film and language today.
items.markingKey: Myths are not meant as factual reports; they express a culture's beliefs, values and ways of understanding the world, and they still shape literature, film and language today. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the special world and the ordinary world.
items.answer: The ordinary world is the hero's normal life at the start of the story; the special world is the unfamiliar, dangerous place the hero enters after crossing the threshold, where the tests happen.
items.markingKey: The ordinary world is the hero's normal life at the start of the story; the special world is the unfamiliar, dangerous place the hero enters after crossing the threshold, where the tests happen. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why modern myths often explain technology or city life.
items.answer: Writers use the old form to make familiar modern things seem magical and to comment on how they affect our lives.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Writers use the old form to make familiar modern things seem magical and to comment on how they affect our lives. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Text A: retelling of the Hindu flood story of Manu and the fish.

One morning, as Manu washed his hands in the river, a tiny fish swam into his palm. 'Protect me,' it begged, 'and one day I will save you.'
Manu kept it in a jar, then a pond, then the sea, for it grew enormous. At last the fish warned him: 'A great flood is coming. Build a boat and take seeds of every plant.'
When the waters rose, the fish – the god Vishnu in disguise – towed Manu's boat to a mountain top. From Manu, the world began again.

Text B: retelling of the Greek flood myth of Deucalion and Pyrrha.

Zeus looked down at humans and saw only cruelty, so he sent rain until the whole world drowned.
Only Deucalion and his wife Pyrrha survived, floating in a wooden chest until it came to rest on Mount Parnassus.
Alone and afraid, they prayed. A voice told them: 'Throw the bones of your mother over your shoulders.'
Pyrrha was horrified – until Deucalion understood. Their mother was the Earth; her bones were stones. Every stone they threw became a person, and the world was full again.

Identify ONE similarity and ONE difference between the two texts, supporting each with a reference to both texts.
items.answer: Similarity: both include a warning or message from a god, a boat or chest that survives the flood, and a new beginning for humanity. Difference: in Text A the flood is survived because Manu was kind to a fish, whereas in Text B the flood is Zeus's punishment and survival depends on solving a riddle.
items.markingKey: Similarity: both include a warning or message from a god, a boat or chest that survives the flood, and a new beginning for humanity. Difference: in Text A the flood is survived because Manu was kind to a fish, whereas in Text B the flood is Zeus's punishment and survival depends on solving a riddle. One mark for each valid, supported point; credit other valid comparisons.

One night a baker's daughter, Ines, heard her crying. 'I'll keep you company,' Ines said, and she lit one lamp in her window.
The Spirit was so grateful that she breathed light into every window, every street and every sign.
And that is why the city never sleeps: it is keeping a lonely spirit company.

Explain what this myth explains and compare it briefly with another myth you know.
items.answer: Why cities stay lit and busy at night: the city is keeping the lonely Night Spirit company.
items.markingKey: Why cities stay lit and busy at night: the city is keeping the lonely Night Spirit company. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Choose a myth or legend you know. Explain how it shows three conventions of the genre, using evidence.
items.answer: Indicative content: identifies three conventions (supernatural beings, explanation of origins, a hero's quest or test, oral storytelling features); supports each with a specific detail; explains what each reveals about the culture.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: identifies three conventions (supernatural beings, explanation of origins, a hero's quest or test, oral storytelling features); supports each with a specific detail; explains what each reveals about the culture.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The hero's journey makes stories predictable."
items.answer: The pattern can feel predictable if used mechanically, but skilled writers use it as a framework and surprise readers within it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: readers recognise stages and can guess what happens; many blockbuster films feel similar. Arguments against: the pattern is flexible and writers vary it; familiar patterns satisfy readers while characters and settings make stories fresh. Supported judgement: The pattern can feel predictable if used mechanically, but skilled writers use it as a framework and surprise readers within it. items.stem: "Modern myths are less meaningful than traditional myths." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Modern myths can be just as meaningful when they explore real modern concerns (loneliness, technology) through the myth form.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: traditional myths carry centuries of cultural belief; modern myths can feel like jokes. Arguments against: modern myths comment on our world and values; all myths were once new. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "pantheon"?
options: All the gods of a particular culture or religion, such as the Greek or Norse gods
A traditional story opening such as "Long ago..." or "In the beginning..." that signals the genre
A wise guide who helps the hero, often with advice or a magical gift
A traditional story, often sacred to a culture, involving gods or supernatural beings, that explains the origins of the world, nature or customs
items.answer: All the gods of a particular culture or religion, such as the Greek or Norse gods
items.markingKey: A. "pantheon" is all the gods of a particular culture or religion, such as the Greek or Norse gods.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The point at which the hero leaves the familiar world and enters the unknown"?
options: archetype
modern myth
call to adventure
threshold
items.answer: threshold
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of threshold.

items.stem: Distinguish between a narrative hook and a formulaic opening.
items.answer: A formulaic opening ("Long ago...") signals the genre through tradition; a narrative hook grabs attention through surprise or mystery. A modern myth can combine both.
items.markingKey: A formulaic opening ("Long ago...") signals the genre through tradition; a narrative hook grabs attention through surprise or mystery. A modern myth can combine both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why comparing myths across cultures is useful.
items.answer: It reveals shared human questions (how did the world begin?) and different cultural values, such as whether the flood is a punishment or a natural disaster.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It reveals shared human questions (how did the world begin?) and different cultural values, such as whether the flood is a punishment or a natural disaster. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a fable and a myth.
items.answer: A myth explains origins or beliefs through gods and heroes; a fable is a short story, often with animals, that teaches a clear moral lesson.
items.markingKey: A myth explains origins or beliefs through gods and heroes; a fable is a short story, often with animals, that teaches a clear moral lesson. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the ordinary world and the special world.
items.answer: The ordinary world is the hero's normal life at the start of the story; the special world is the unfamiliar, dangerous place the hero enters after crossing the threshold, where the tests happen.
items.markingKey: The ordinary world is the hero's normal life at the start of the story; the special world is the unfamiliar, dangerous place the hero enters after crossing the threshold, where the tests happen. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "The "And that is why..." ending is too childish for a modern myth." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The explanatory ending is a defining convention of origin myths; writers can use it playfully or seriously to give the story its purpose.
items.markingKey: The explanatory ending is a defining convention of origin myths; writers can use it playfully or seriously to give the story its purpose. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph comparing two flood myths, using a comparative connective.
items.answer: For example: "Whereas the Greek flood is a punishment from Zeus, the flood in the Manu story is survived through kindness, showing different ideas about why disaster comes."
items.markingKey: For example: "Whereas the Greek flood is a punishment from Zeus, the flood in the Manu story is survived through kindness, showing different ideas about why disaster comes."

items.stem:
Read the following retelling of the Chinese creation myth of Pangu.

In the beginning there was only a great egg, and inside it slept Pangu.
For eighteen thousand years he grew, until one day he stretched and the egg cracked open. The light, clear parts floated up and became the sky; the heavy, dark parts sank and became the earth.
Afraid they would join again, Pangu stood between them, pushing the sky higher each day.
When at last he died, his breath became the wind, his voice the thunder, his eyes the sun and moon, and his blood the rivers.

What does this story suggest about the values of the culture that created it?
items.answer: It suggests a belief that people and nature are connected: the world is literally made from a body, and creation comes from sacrifice and hard work.
items.markingKey: It suggests a belief that people and nature are connected: the world is literally made from a body, and creation comes from sacrifice and hard work. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: "Every story must follow all twelve stages of the hero's journey in exact order." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The hero's journey is a flexible pattern; many stories skip, combine or reorder stages.
items.markingKey: The hero's journey is a flexible pattern; many stories skip, combine or reorder stages. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Plan a modern myth explaining why phones need charging every night: name the hero, the supernatural being, the challenge and the explanation at the end.
items.answer: Any coherent plan: a hero (e.g. a girl who stays up too late), a being (e.g. the Battery Spirit), a challenge or bargain, and an ending ("And that is why...").
items.markingKey: Any coherent plan: a hero (e.g. a girl who stays up too late), a being (e.g. the Battery Spirit), a challenge or bargain, and an ending ("And that is why...").

items.stem: A student claims: "Cultures with similar myths must have copied each other." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Similar myths can develop independently because people everywhere face similar experiences (floods, darkness, the sky) and ask similar questions.
items.markingKey: Similar myths can develop independently because people everywhere face similar experiences (floods, darkness, the sky) and ask similar questions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Myths are still relevant to teenagers today."
items.answer: Myths remain relevant because their patterns and themes still shape stories and help us explore what it means to be human, even if we no longer read them as explanations of nature.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: modern films and books (superhero stories, fantasy) use mythical heroes and quests; myths explore universal themes like courage, family and loss. Arguments against: science now explains nature; some myths reflect old-fashioned values. Supported judgement: Myths remain relevant because their patterns and themes still shape stories and help us explore what it means to be human, even if we no longer read them as explanations of nature.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a fishing boat returning to a harbour in Ghana at sunset; children run along the beach towards it.]

Write a descriptive piece of about 300 words inspired by this image.
items.answer: Indicative content: a father's return, a first catch, or a village celebration; structure – waiting on the beach – the boat appears – the welcome; techniques such as colour imagery, sound, a rising tempo; a joyful and warm mood.
